title: Dental implant treatment
blurb: What an implant is, the stages from assessment to restoration, osseointegration, the nurse's surgical role, and the complications and maintenance that keep implants healthy.
question: A patient had an implant crown fitted on 36 two years ago. At his review the gum round it bleeds, and a radiograph shows bone loss round the implant threads. He smokes and admits he rarely cleans between his teeth. What is happening, and what advice will help?

teach.body: A dental implant is a screw-shaped post, usually titanium, placed into the jawbone to act as an artificial root. It has three parts: the implant body (fixture) in the bone, an abutment that connects to it through the gum, and the restoration on top. Implants can replace a single tooth, support a bridge, or hold a denture firmly in place. Dental nurses who specialise can take the NEBDN Certificate in Dental Implant Nursing.

root.label: Implant (fixture in bone)
root.sub: Abutment connects it to the mouth

children.label: Overdenture
children.sub: Clips onto studs or a bar

teach.body: Osseointegration is the direct structural and functional connection between living bone and the implant surface. There is no periodontal ligament, so the implant is fused to the bone. It takes time, usually several months, and needs a gentle surgical technique: drilling is irrigated with sterile saline so the bone doesn't overheat, and the implant must stay still while it heals. Smoking, uncontrolled diabetes, poor oral hygiene, radiotherapy to the jaws and some bone medicines all raise the risk of failure.

steps.label: Surgical placement
steps.sub: Implant placed in bone under sterile conditions

steps.label: Restoration
steps.sub: Impression or scan, then crown, bridge or denture fitted

steps.label: Maintenance
steps.sub: Home care and regular reviews for life

teach.caption: If there isn't enough bone, grafting or a sinus lift may be needed first. Some implants are restored sooner, at the clinician's judgement.

items: Set up a sterile field: sterile gowns, gloves, drapes and a surgical aspirator tip.
Prepare the implant motor with sterile saline irrigation and check the surgical kit is complete.
Confirm the implant system and size with the surgeon before opening it.
Pass the implant without touching its surface: contamination stops it integrating.
Record the implant's batch (lot) number and details in the notes so it can be traced.
Monitor the patient, then give written post-operative instructions.

teach.caption: Untreated peri-implantitis can end in the implant being lost. Smoking and poor plaque control are major risk factors.

teach.body: Early problems include swelling, bleeding, infection, the implant failing to integrate, and, in the lower jaw, damage to the nerve that causes numbness or tingling of the lip or chin. Later problems include peri-implant disease, a loose abutment screw, and a chipped or fractured crown. Patients should report numbness that persists after the anaesthetic should have worn off, a loose crown or a bleeding gum round an implant, so the clinician can see them.

Implants need cleaning as carefully as natural teeth. Show patients how to brush round the implant crown, clean underneath it with interdental brushes or implant floss, and use a single-tufted brush along the gum. Encourage stopping smoking. Regular reviews let the clinician check the gum, the bite and, when prescribed, the bone level on a radiograph. Professional cleaning uses instruments that won't scratch the implant surface.

teach.text: Implants can't decay, so patients sometimes think they don't need cleaning. They do: plaque causes peri-implant mucositis and then peri-implantitis, which destroys the bone holding the implant.

items: Implant body in bone, abutment through the gum, restoration on top.
Osseointegration: bone fuses directly to the implant over several months.
Sterile set-up, saline irrigation, no-touch handling, record the batch number.
Mucositis = gum only, reversible. Peri-implantitis = bone loss, can lose the implant.
Daily cleaning, no smoking and regular reviews keep implants healthy.

summary: You can now describe the parts of an implant, explain osseointegration and what threatens it, list the stages from assessment to maintenance, carry out the nurse's role at surgery, and tell peri-implant mucositis from peri-implantitis.

A.q: What does the term osseointegration describe?
options: The gum attaching to a new crown
Cement sealing the abutment in place
A ligament forming round the implant
Bone bonding directly to the implant
A.why: Osseointegration is the direct structural and functional connection between living bone and the implant surface.

whyNot.0: Gum healing round the abutment is soft tissue healing, not osseointegration.
whyNot.1: Cement may hold a crown on, but osseointegration is about bone and implant.
whyNot.2: Implants have no periodontal ligament; bone contacts the implant directly.

A.q: During implant surgery, why is sterile saline run through the implant motor while drilling?
options: To numb the bone during drilling
To help the gum heal faster
A.why: Heat from drilling can kill bone cells and prevent osseointegration, so the drill is cooled with sterile saline.

whyNot.0: Local anaesthetic numbs the area; saline doesn't.
whyNot.2: Irrigation protects bone; it doesn't speed gum healing.
whyNot.3: The implant arrives sterile; saline is not a disinfectant.

A.q: An implant crown has red, bleeding gum round it, but the radiograph shows no bone loss. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A.why: Inflammation limited to the soft tissue, with no bone loss, is peri-implant mucositis, which is reversible.

whyNot.1: Peri-implantitis includes bone loss round the implant.
whyNot.2: Failed integration usually shows as a mobile implant, not inflamed gum alone.
whyNot.3: A fractured abutment causes looseness, not gum inflammation with intact bone.

B.q: While opening an implant at surgery, what must the nurse avoid?
B.why: The implant surface must not be touched, even with sterile gloves, because contamination can stop osseointegration.

whyNot.0: Checking the size with the surgeon before opening is good practice.
whyNot.1: The batch number must be recorded for traceability.
whyNot.3: The implant is handed or loaded for the surgeon using a no-touch technique.

B.q: Which factor most increases the risk of an implant failing?
B.why: Smoking impairs healing and blood supply and is strongly linked with implant failure and peri-implantitis.

whyNot.0: A mouthguard protects teeth and has no harmful effect on implants.
whyNot.1: Electric brushes help plaque control round implants.
whyNot.2: Fluoride toothpaste is safe to use with implants.

B.q: Which part of an implant connects the implant body in the bone to the crown?
B.why: The abutment passes through the gum and connects the implant body to the restoration.

whyNot.0: The fixture is the implant body that sits in the bone.
whyNot.2: A pontic is the false tooth in a bridge.
whyNot.3: A retainer is the part of a bridge fixed to an abutment tooth.

C.q: Why is the implant's batch (lot) number recorded in the patient's notes?
options: So the implant can be traced if there is a recall
So the practice can order a matching shade
So the lab knows which crown cement to use
So the patient's fees can be calculated
C.why: Recording the batch number means the patient can be identified and contacted if that batch is ever subject to a safety notice or recall.

whyNot.1: Shade is recorded separately and doesn't depend on the implant batch.
whyNot.2: The batch number doesn't decide the choice of crown cement.
whyNot.3: Fees are not calculated from the batch number.

C.q: A patient two weeks after lower implant surgery says his lip on that side is still numb. What should the nurse do?
options: Reassure him it will settle on its own
Book him in at his routine annual review
Advise him to massage the lip each day
Tell the clinician so he can be assessed
C.why: Persisting numbness after lower implant surgery can mean nerve injury, so the clinician needs to assess him promptly.

whyNot.0: Nurses can't diagnose; prolonged numbness needs clinical assessment.
whyNot.1: Waiting a year could make any nerve damage harder to manage.
whyNot.2: Massage won't help and delays assessment of a possible nerve injury.

C.q: Which statement about peri-implantitis is correct?
options: It affects only the gum and is reversible
It is decay in the crown on the implant
It involves bone loss round the implant
It happens only in the first week after surgery
C.why: Peri-implantitis is inflammation with loss of supporting bone round the implant, and it can lead to implant loss.

whyNot.0: Gum-only, reversible inflammation is peri-implant mucositis.
whyNot.1: Implant crowns and implants can't decay.
whyNot.3: Peri-implantitis usually develops months or years after treatment.

reteach.title: A fence post set in concrete
reteach.question: Think about a fence post set in concrete. Why must it be left alone while the concrete sets, and what would rot it later?

blocks.body: The implant is the post and the bone is the concrete. If you wobble the post or pour concrete that's too hot, it never sets solid: that's why the bone is kept cool with saline and the implant left to heal for months. Once it's set, the post lasts as long as you keep the ground round it healthy. Plaque at the gum line is like water pooling at the base: first the surface gets soggy (mucositis), then the concrete crumbles (peri-implantitis).

items.label: Clean daily, review regularly
items.sub: Plaque leads to mucositis, then peri-implantitis

blocks.text: Natural teeth have a periodontal ligament; implants don't. That's why an implant feels rigid and why it can't move with orthodontic treatment.

explain.body: The implant body (fixture) sits in bone, the abutment connects it through the gum, and a crown, bridge or overdenture goes on top.

test.q: Which part of the implant system sits in the jawbone?
test.why: The fixture (implant body) is the screw that is placed in the bone.

whyNot.0: The abutment sits on the fixture and passes through the gum.
whyNot.1: The crown sits on the abutment in the mouth.
whyNot.3: A healing cap sits on top of the implant while the gum heals.

explain.body: Bone grows directly onto the implant surface over several months. It needs cool, gentle surgery, a clean implant surface and a stable implant. Smoking, uncontrolled diabetes and poor hygiene raise the failure risk.

test.q: Which of these is most likely to prevent osseointegration?
options: The patient using a soft toothbrush
Saline used to cool the drill
test.why: Movement during healing stops bone fusing to the implant, leading to fibrous tissue instead.

whyNot.1: A soft brush helps keep the area clean without harm.
whyNot.2: Saline cooling protects the bone and helps integration.
whyNot.3: A radiograph checks position; it doesn't affect healing.

explain.body: Sterile field, sterile saline irrigation, complete kit, confirm the implant size, no-touch handling, record the batch number, monitor the patient and give written aftercare.

items.label: recorded in the notes for traceability

test.q: What is used to cool the drill during implant site preparation?
test.why: Sterile saline is used because it is sterile and isotonic, so it cools the bone without harming it.

whyNot.0: Dental unit water isn't sterile and isn't suitable for surgical irrigation.
whyNot.2: Chlorhexidine is an antiseptic rinse, not an irrigant for drilling bone.
whyNot.3: Distilled water from the unit bottle isn't sterile for surgery.

explain.body: Peri-implant mucositis affects the gum only and is reversible. Peri-implantitis destroys bone and can lose the implant. Daily cleaning with interdental brushes, not smoking and regular reviews prevent both.

test.q: Which home-care advice is best for a patient with an implant bridge?
options: Clean under it daily with interdental brushes
Rinse with water instead of brushing it
Leave it alone as implants can't decay
Brush it once a week with whitening paste
test.why: Plaque under an implant bridge causes peri-implant disease, so it must be cleaned daily with interdental brushes or implant floss.

whyNot.2: Implants can't decay but can be lost to peri-implantitis.
whyNot.3: Weekly brushing is far too little, and abrasive pastes can scratch.
